strengths: Well-motivated, practical problem addressing real C-to-Rust migration challenges
Sensible two-step methodology clearly separating semantic preservation from idiomaticity refinement
Novel FFI-based end-to-end verification approach that is more practical than symbolic execution or fuzz testing
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across two datasets, five LLMs, with detailed cost and failure analysis
Strong empirical results: up to 93% success rate (DeepSeek-R1) with 100% unsafe-free output
Valuable failure categorization providing insights into model-specific strengths (e.g., DeepSeek-R1's robustness on complex code)
Good reproducibility practices with promised code/dataset release and detailed LLM configurations
weaknesses: FUNDAMENTAL ISSUE—Out of scope for ACL: This is a software engineering/systems application paper, not a computational linguistics contribution. It uses LLMs as tools to solve an SE problem but makes no contribution to NLP, language understanding, or LLM capabilities. Should be submitted to ICSE/FSE/ASE instead

Limited evaluation scope: Started with 698/750k+ programs, filtered to 100 total; aggressive filtering for compilation/memory errors likely biases toward easier cases; no justification for 'most LOC' selection criterion

Verification limitations: 'Soft equivalence' via end-to-end tests ≠ functional correctness; relies on test quality; case studies show LLM-generated test harnesses frequently fail; auto-generated tests (CodeNet) not validated

No ablation studies: Why C2Rust only for types? Why exactly 6 retries? Why these static analysis tools? No single-step baseline. No measurement of whether static analysis hints actually improve results

Weak baseline comparison: Baselines have different design goals; Vert only evaluated on one dataset; Figure 7 shows unidiomatic SACTOR already beats all baselines, suggesting improvements from LLM use rather than methodology
Failure categorization lacks rigor: No inter-rater reliability metrics; manual verification after DeepSeek-R1 categorization introduces bias; some category overlaps not addressed; process unclear
Cost analysis incomplete: DeepSeek-R1 costs 5-7× more tokens than GPT-4o but marginal gains not justified; no monetary cost provided; token/query relationship under-explained

Weak real-world generalization: Only 2 case studies; urlparser described as 'simple'; avl_tree has significant failures (10/23 functions); no evidence of scaling to large real-world projects like Linux kernel
Missing statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; LLM variance not analyzed; small post-filtering sample sizes
Limited model analysis: Observes reasoning models perform better but provides no deep investigation into why; no analysis of prompt sensitivity; no few-shot vs. zero-shot comparison
Reproducibility concerns: Closed-source LLMs may change/disappear; no variance analysis across multiple runs; test harness generation failure rate not reported

strengths: Well-motivated, practical problem with clear security/safety benefits for C-to-Rust migration
Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 200+ programs, 5 LLMs, multiple datasets, detailed failure analysis with categorization
Sound two-step methodology: unidiomatic (semantic preservation) → idiomatic (safety/idiomaticity) is principled problem decomposition
Novel FFI-based end-to-end verification approach is more practical for real-world code than symbolic execution/fuzz testing
Strong empirical results: 93% success rate (DeepSeek-R1), 100% unsafe-free translations, outperforms 4 baselines on idiomaticity
Valuable insight that reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1) outperform on complex code with intricate logic/arrays
Practical cost analysis (token consumption, query counts) provides actionable guidance
Clear presentation with effective figures, examples, and comprehensive appendices
weaknesses: Limited scope for ACL (computational linguistics): This is a software engineering paper; does not advance NLP/LLM methodology or theory, better suited for ICSE/PLDI/ASE
Not genuinely 'zero-shot': Heavily dependent on static analysis tools (libclang, C2Rust, Crown); hybrid neuro-symbolic approach obscures independent LLM contribution; missing ablation studies
Limited novelty in LLM methodology: Standard prompting techniques (context, dependencies, error feedback); no insights into code understanding or novel prompting strategies

Verification limitations: 'Soft equivalence' (E2E test success) is not comprehensive correctness guarantee; CodeNet test generator details largely absent; unresolved challenges in case studies (function pointers, harness generation)

Dataset/sampling concerns: TransCoder-IR selects only longest 100/698 programs (potential bias); CodeNet only 100/750k+ with restrictive filtering; real-world evaluation: only 2 projects insufficient for generalization
Missing ablation studies: No quantitative assessment of C2Rust vs. Crown vs. LLM contributions independently; single-stage vs. two-stage comparison absent
Insufficient statistical rigor: No confidence intervals, significance tests, or variance reporting; only one run per program; small real-world sample
Cost-performance tradeoff unaddressed: DeepSeek-R1 requires 5-7× more tokens than GPT-4o; cost analysis excludes failed attempts (biased)
Missing implementation details: SACTOR test generator for CodeNet (creation/validation methodology), adaptive prompting rules, C Parser design/limitations underexplained
Reproducibility concerns: Code/dataset URLs redacted; LLM versions change over time; inherent challenges with LLM-based research reproducibility not fully addressed

strengths: Two-stage pipeline elegantly separates semantic preservation from idiomatic refinement, providing a generalizable design pattern for code transformation
Comprehensive evaluation across 200+ programs and real-world codebases (CRust-Bench, libogg) with 6 LLM models and detailed failure categorization (5-7 categories per dataset)
Significant idiomaticity improvements: 100% unsafe-free translations vs 0-45.6% for baselines; 0.28 avg Clippy alerts/function vs 1.60-2.96 for rule-based methods
Pragmatic FFI-based E2E verification with SPEC-driven harness generation avoids infeasible symbolic execution while enabling practical validation
Strong integration of static analysis (C2Rust, Crown, custom C Parser) to guide LLM prompts, with ablation studies demonstrating 17% contribution from Crown
Honest assessment of limitations including test coverage dependence, model variance, unsupported C features, and harness generation stability
weaknesses: Fundamental scope mismatch: This is a software engineering/program synthesis paper, not a computational linguistics or NLP contribution. Venue should be ICSE/FSE/ASE, not ACL.

Overstated correctness claims: 'Soft equivalence' via E2E testing cannot guarantee formal correctness. Untested paths may contain bugs; C undefined behavior and Rust safety gaps create undetectable mismatches.
Moderate real-world performance: CRust-Bench shows only 25% fully idiomatic (8/32 samples); libogg 53-78% idiomatic success. Majority of translations require manual intervention for production use.

Statistical rigor absent: No confidence intervals, significance tests, or single-pass success rates (6 retries inflates reported success); trivial baseline gets 10 attempts vs SACTOR's 6, unfairly favoring SACTOR.

Reproducibility compromised: Code repository link incomplete; proprietary LLM dependency (GPT-4o/GPT-5); CRust-Bench from 2025 (unstable); SPEC/harness implementation details scattered across appendices.

Soft equivalence limitations underexplored: E2E testing provides no coverage guarantees; Table 14 shows many runtime/compile failures despite 'passing' translations, indicating false positives in verification.
